title: The Warm Cage
passages:
Teodoro read it out loud, all of it, because that was how he read anything, and nobody at Anza asked him a question they didn't want the whole shop to hear.

"Hold order," he said. "Remand of the live lid-hand, Bay Four, to the coast roster. Collecting vehicle already logged." He tilted the plate so the cathode light bleeding under the back-room door ran across the glass. "Filed at the Kettering morning desk, 05:40."

The plate was the node's list of its own people — name, badge, status — and under each one a strip of small gray type that a desk four hundred kilometers off could write to without asking anybody's leave. Reader two sat below it, the block that read a body's hands and voice and put a name where there hadn't been one. It had put Wren's there an hour ago. She sat against the compressor housing with her wrists still bound in seal tape, saying *thirty-six point four* under her breath, the way a pump says its own pressure.

"There's a second part," Teodoro said.

"Of course there is." Rhea had a respirator cartridge in one fist and grease to the elbow and no intention of putting either down.

"File 2244. Physical recovery. Badge 2244." He read it twice, which he only did when a line surprised him. "It's moving. Deadline pinned to the shift bell."

Behind him the compressor held its note. Ivo was on the other side of that note, on mains power, breathing through a disc of heavy glove rubber cut out of a palm — except the palm belonged to the woman on the floor and the man it was cut around was alive in the next room.

"Chain condition," Teodoro said, and stopped.

"Teodoro."

"Green holds while the remand is executed." He looked up. "It's the food line, Rhea. She rolls at the bell, Anza eats. She doesn't, and the chain drops red at the bell with Brill's canisters still sitting on the truck at the ore stub."

"Eleven seals short," Nour said from the board ledge, not moving, "and now we're short a person."

Coombs stood in the shop doorway with the cold coming in around his boots and said nothing at all, which Rhea distrusted more than talk. Out in the yard his tender rang the quarter. It had a warm sound, that bell, like a kitchen.

"There's a signature field," Teodoro said. "It wants a countersigning badge."

"Fine. Whose?"

"It's already filled in." He turned the plate around so she could see it.

*2244.*

Through the back-room door came the scrape of a boot on plank, and Marlowe's voice, thick with the sedative still coming off him. "Is that the desk? Tell them I'm not signing myself off."

"Nobody's asking you to," Rhea said, to the door, and then, lower, to the plate: "It's not asking him to sign. It's asking us to sign *her*, and it's holding his number over the field like a hand over a stove."

Wren had stopped counting. In the quiet she looked at the glass, at the four digits sitting there, and Rhea watched her understand it a half second before anyone said it out loud — that the desk had made it one trade with two names on it, and that the bell was going to take one of them either way.

"Two days," Teodoro said, because he told you everything he knew. "Recovery's window is two days from the filing. But the deadline's the bell."

The cursor went on blinking under Marlowe's badge. Out in the yard the tender's bell rang again, closer to warm than before, and the plate waited for somebody standing in that room to put a name under it.
